prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Security advisories for affected dependencies (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 13px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "CVE ID" · longest unbreakable word 41px · one-line width 110px
  col 2: header "Package" · longest unbreakable word 144px · one-line width 144px
  col 3: header "Affected versions" · longest unbreakable word 55px · one-line width 297px
  col 4: header "Severity" · longest unbreakable word 52px · one-line width 52px
  col 5: header "Summary" · longest unbreakable word 195px · one-line width 2738px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 793px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 792px.
Fixed: content, font, 13px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 793px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Help readers identify vulnerable dependencies, assess severity, and determine whether their installed versions are affected.","reading":"Readers can scan CVE IDs, packages, and severity, then compare version ranges and read the relevant summary. Long summaries will often set row height, leaving room for version ranges to wrap within the same row.","groups":["CVE ID and Package identify the advisory and dependency.","Affected versions and Package work together to determine exposure.","Severity and Summary convey urgency and describe the issue."],"keep_intact":["CVE identifiers","Package names, including slash-separated paths","Individual version numbers and comparison operators","Severity labels"],"may_wrap":["Affected version ranges at spaces or between comma-separated ranges","Summary prose at word boundaries","The Affected versions header"]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[131,165,207,73,216],"idea":"Give version ranges the most room while keeping the summary wide enough for its longest unbreakable word."},{"name":"B","widths":[131,165,165,73,258],"idea":"Balance version-range readability with a wider summary, using summary-driven row height to absorb some range wrapping."},{"name":"C","widths":[131,165,135,73,288],"idea":"Prioritize summary prose and accept more wrapping in the affected-version ranges while preserving the identifying columns."}]}
